To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
instrumental variables can be used to infer causality and that they are a useful tool in the epidemiologist’s toolbox, but they should only be used with caution.

the instrumental variable method is an approach to estimate causal effects that can be used in observational data, but requires four identifying assumptions that can only partly be validated empirically.

the instrumental variable method is used to estimate causal effects in observational studies and that it can only be applied when four assumptions hold: (i) the instrument must be associated with the exposure, (ii) the instrument must not be associated with the outcome, (iii) there must be a non-zero effect of the exposure on the outcome, (iv) there must be no unmeasured confounder that is associated with both the exposure and the outcome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What is an instrumental variable and why should we use it?
the development and application of methods for estimating causal effects in the presence of confounding, with a focus on instrumental variables.
developing methods for causal inference in observational studies, with a focus on the use of instrumental variables.

the instrument is associated with the exposure, but is independent of the unmeasured confounder, and that the instrument identifies a subgroup of the population where the effect of the exposure on the outcome is independent of the confounder.
the instrument satisfies the four identifying assumptions and that the estimated effect is generalisable.

an instrument is a variable, that is associated with exposure, but not associated with the outcome conditional on exposure and that is associated with unmeasured confounder(s) conditional on exposure.

the instrument is not a magic bullet, but an additional tool that can be employed to increase the precision of causal estimates in settings with unmeasured confounds.
